R002

The genealogy is more complex than a one-way export from Andalusia to America: it is better understood as an iterative Atlantic system in which institutions, capital, people, and techniques crossed repeatedly in both directions. The first decisive Andalusian episode is 1248, not 1238: after Ferdinand III conquered Seville, the repartimiento transferred Muslim property to Christian settlers, nobles, ecclesiastical corporations, and military orders. Importantly, González Jiménez’s documentary reconstruction corrects the old picture of an immediately latifundist settlement: small and medium proprietors initially received most holdings. The decisive concentration came afterward. Between roughly 1240 and 1300, military insecurity, depopulation, labor shortages, and economic distress caused settlers to abandon or sell land into a market in which supply greatly exceeded demand; wealthy purchasers and institutions could therefore aggregate numerous cheap parcels into cortijos and large patrimonies. Thus conquest created the property rupture, while a subsequent land market produced much of the concentration. González Jiménez finds examples of military orders acquiring thousands of fanegas through purchase, exchange, and donation. (González Jiménez, 1980). 

The sixteenth-century Atlantic economy then supplied a second concentration mechanism. Pike showed that fortunes made through Seville’s privileged American commerce were converted into estates in the Aljarafe and Sierra Morena and into mayorazgos: merchant capital literally became landed aristocratic wealth (Pike, 1965). Thus colonial accumulation did not originate Andalusian latifundism, but it increased the purchasing power available to consolidate land and enabled merchants to become absentee landed elites. 

I would now qualify sharply what I previously said about the hacienda returning from America. I cannot find good evidence that the characteristically American labor institutions—particularly indigenous tribute labor, encomienda-derived coercion, or debt peonage—were subsequently transplanted wholesale into Andalusia. Those were genuinely colonial elaborations, especially the combination of large estates with indigenous communities, peonaje por deudas, and ethnically differentiated coercive jurisdictions (Lockhart, 1969; Mörner, 1973). The demonstrable reverse transmission is stronger for capital, proprietors, commercial orientation, Atlantic slavery, consumption patterns, and estate investment than for a particular American labor regime. Andalusian cortijo/hacienda organization and seasonal jornalero labor therefore resulted from convergent and reciprocally interacting Atlantic developments, not simple institutional reimportation. 

There is a clearer Iberian-to-colonial continuity in religious classification as a technology of rule. After the 1264 Mudéjar revolt, much of the Muslim population of lower Andalusia was expelled; Jews faced violence and mass conversion beginning dramatically in 1391 and the convert-or-expel decree of 1492; Granada’s Muslims were progressively coerced into conversion after 1499, culminating in compulsory conversion or departure in Castile. Christianity increasingly became a condition of legitimate membership in the polity—although conversos and Moriscos remained discriminated against through limpieza de sangre. García-Arenal and Crewe identify Granada and the Canaries as important precedents for American conquest-and-conversion regimes; this is a much stronger institutional continuity than any claimed return of encomienda to Andalusia (García-Arenal, 1992; Crewe, 2006). 

Finally, liberal capitalism supplied another major ratchet. Beginning with Carlos IV’s 1798 desamortización, and much more dramatically under Mendizábal from 1836 and Madoz in 1855, ecclesiastical, entailed, municipal, and common resources were marketized. Because land was sold rather than redistributed, people possessing liquid capital could purchase it while jornaleros generally could not; privatization also removed common grazing, gathering, and cultivation rights that had supplemented wages. The result in western Andalusia was not simply “feudal persistence” but an increasingly capitalist latifundist agriculture employing propertyless wage labor (Herr, 1989; Malefakis, 1970). 

That social structure helps explain why anarchism and later anarcho-syndicalism acquired an exceptional rural base in Andalusia from the First International onward. Cádiz–Jerez and the lower Guadalquivir became major centers; organizers could mobilize landless seasonal laborers around direct action, wage struggles, land access, and hostility to both landlords and the state. By 1918–1920 the CNT/FNOA current had tens of thousands of Andalusian agricultural adherents, although it competed increasingly with the socialist UGT. Andalusia therefore did not merely receive Spanish anarcho-syndicalism: its jornalero society became one of the environments in which Spanish libertarian syndicalism acquired its distinctive agrarian form (Montañés & Simpson, 2015; Sánchez Castillo, 2020).

comments.author: @JJ-fr2ki
comments.text:
Scholarly disagreement about 3/3 regions: Describing Andalusia’s earlier wealth as evidence of superior productive development is misleading. The region has excellent natural agricultural endowments—fertile land, a Mediterranean climate, and in some areas sophisticated irrigation—but its agriculture has historically been constrained by concentrated landholding, low capital investment, extensive rather than intensive cultivation, seasonal labor, and comparatively weak mechanization. Natural agricultural wealth is not the same thing as high agricultural productivity.

Those structural weaknesses mattered enormously. Andalusia had the potential for something closer to California-style high-productivity agriculture, but large estates and unequal landholding often provided weak incentives for labor-saving investment and broad-based capital formation. Even today, although parts of Andalusian agriculture are technologically advanced, the sector as a whole should not be confused with the frontier of capital-intensive agriculture represented by the most highly automated farming systems in places such as the United States, Australia, Israel, or the Netherlands.

Conversely, describing Catalonia and the Basque Country as simply poor regions before nineteenth-century industrialization is misleading. Catalonia already possessed substantial commercial and proto-industrial development in the eighteenth century and was mechanizing cotton production by the 1790s. The Basque Country likewise had a centuries-old ironworking, mining, shipbuilding, and commercial economy well before the nineteenth-century steel boom.

Bessemer technology was enormously important because low-phosphorus Biscayan ore was exceptionally well suited to the process, but it accelerated an existing metallurgical economy rather than creating Basque industry from nothing. The precise history of coke supply is more complicated: British imports became very important, especially given Biscay’s excellent maritime connections, while other regional sources also appear in accounts of the industry.

The modern economic geography is consistent with this longer history. Catalonia and the Basque Country remain substantially richer and more productive than Andalusia, although simple wage comparisons are misleading because taxes, employment rates, public benefits, household structure, and regional prices differ. The safer comparison is regional output and purchasing power: both Catalonia and especially the Basque Country remain far above Andalusia.

So the historical trajectory is not “rich Andalusia versus impoverished Catalonia and the Basque Country until nineteenth-century industrialization.” Catalonia and the Basque Country already possessed unusually developed commercial and productive economies, while Andalusia combined exceptional natural agricultural resources with institutions and investment patterns that repeatedly produced much less efficient agriculture than those resources should have supported.

replies.text:
@GeographyEffect Good work. I reacted too antagonistically because of the AI slop issue, which is a poor excuse for a breach of scholarly etiquette norms. I have made some changes to my original comments. Two subtle issues where we diverge remain.
First, fertile land—even when high-yielding—does not equate to high-productivity farming. The latter concerns human utilization, an area where Spain has struggled since the expulsion of the Moors. Exploitative labor practices, inheritance structures that reduce incentives, and the slow adoption of contemporaneous state-of-the-art techniques all testify to this low efficiency.
Second, do not count out the Catalans. I do not know the exact reason (perhaps an anthropologist has an account. To be clear, I am not engaging in essentialism—nor am I suggesting that the Spanish are lazy—but rather reinforcing a fact reflected in economic data and observed by nearly every foreigner residing in Spain long enough). Catalonia was quick to industrialize and served as a wealthy commercial center even before the late 17th century, operating as a maritime power trading with Florence during the Renaissance. Returning to my earlier caveats, there appears to be something specific to Catalan culture—such as a tendency toward entrepreneurship and business efficacy—that distinguishes them from other Spaniards in this regard.
To review: good land does not imply real wealth for its inhabitants, nor does it indicate productive land use. The Catalan and Basque regions were never particularly poor, except during periods of plague or civil war, and even then, they rebounded relatively quickly. Napoleon did not even attempt to manage the Basques, and Franco, at his strongest, was unable to extract much beyond customs duties. Furthermore, after the assassination, he failed to shut down the Mondragon Corporation; instead, he was forced to support it because of its economic productivity, particularly in industrial sectors prioritized by the admiralty.
If I have made errors—and I am sure I have made a few here—they might stem from my insistence on an anthropology of Spanish activity across different territories that deliberately discounts colonial injections of wealth. Such injections produce a distorted picture of the economy and the daily lives of ordinary people in Spain. A critic might push back on this—I can easily envision certain Spanish conservatives arguing this point—by asserting that what I regard as a thuggish genocide should instead be viewed as a source of wealth production by a subset of ethnic Spaniards, deserving recognition as a form of economic success. They would argue that I am allowing normative commitments to interfere with objective economic history.
I wish to avoid that trap, so my brief defense is this: the video and my discussion have focused on the lives and productivity of the Spanish within Spain. Your analysis, for example, by focusing on the customs house, makes parts of Spain appear richer. However, that wealth was narrowly distributed among families and was not generated by actual wealth creation by Spaniards, as it was in the Catalan and Basque regions.
Regarding Speculations on a Railroad
A single rail line from Barcelona to Bilbao—offered here as a speculative thesis—could have done an enormous amount to accelerate and modernize Spain. The country was actually fairly early to industrialize on both a European and global scale. Standard historical accounts tend to overemphasize politics; however, the under-investment in new railroads, and the insistence on treating Madrid as the central hub, were fundamentally political errors. Directly linking the most productive regions of Spain would have been immensely valuable.
